title: Science Factionalism: How Group Identity Language Affects Public Engagement With Misinformation and Debunking Narratives on a Popular Q&A Platform in China
screen_reason: The paper's aim is the effect of group identity language on engagement, not prevalence, but its content analysis reports the descriptive composition of the corpus in Table 1: of 5,858 GMO answers on Zhihu, 374 were coded as propagating GMO misinformation (and 4,049 were misinformation-irrelevant, 992 debunking, 443 ambiguous). 374/5,858 is an exact part/whole share from verbatim counts with the same denominator (they sum exactly to the stated Full Sample N), so it is keepable under R8 and gives one CONTENT estimate. Everything else in the paper is identity-language, negativity, justification or regression output.

estimates.platform: Zhihu (popular Chinese Q&A platform, 'like its American counterpart Quora')
estimates.date: Eight-year time series of Zhihu GMO answers, crawled 'as of September 2019'
estimates.measure_type: % of GMO-related Zhihu answers that propagated GMO misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 374/5,858 = 6.4% (Table 1: Full Sample N = 5858; Propagate Misinformation N = 374; the four columns 4049 + 374 + 992 + 443 sum exactly to 5858)
estimates.denominator: 5,858 GMO-related Zhihu answers written by the 221 most active GMO authors (those with more than 10 GMO answers), out of the 6,039 answers content-analysed; 181 dropped because the comment-count indicator was unavailable
estimates.definition: An answer was coded 'Mention Misinformation' if it discussed any of four types of GMO-related misinformation, and then 'Propagate Misinformation' if it showed agreement with that misinformation (as opposed to 'Debunk' - disagreement - or 'Ambiguous Attitude' - neither).
estimates.misinfo_def: "To determine whether GMO misinformation is mentioned in each answer, we referred to common misinformation and corresponding scientific facts about GMO summarized by the Chinese Agricultural Biosafety Management Office, the China Association for Science and Technology (China MOA, 2014), and other literature... an answer discussed any of the four types of GMO-related misinformation: (1) the false health risk of GM food, (2) the fake environment effects from GMO plantation, (3) people's misperception of government regulation of GMO, and (4) GMO-related international political misinformation."

estimates.page_loc: Table 1 and its table note, p. 7
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two researchers manually annotated all 6,039 answers against a reference list of common GMO misinformation and the corresponding scientific facts compiled by the Chinese Agricultural Biosafety Management Office and the China Association for Science and Technology (China MOA, 2014), supplemented by other literature (China CDC 2015; Huang et al. 2006; Liang & Xing 2015; Yan 2012). Reported reliability: 'the intercoder agreement for each variable is high, ranging from 0.812 to 1 using Cohen's kappa coefficient'; no per-variable kappa is broken out. Codebook in Supplemental Material Appendix I (not available in this text).
estimates.moderator_quote: We used the Zhihu Web Crawler API to collect all the answers about GM (转基因), which result in 40,101 answers posted by more than 21,422 unique users as of September 2019. Then we chose the users that have posted more than 10 GMO-related answers and got 221 unique authors who have written 6039 answers in total for in-depth content analysis. [English: the corpus is a single-issue GMO keyword crawl, purposively narrowed to the most prolific answerers.]
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALLS FOR THE ADJUDICATOR. (1) The 6.4% is DERIVED, not printed: the paper never states a percentage of the corpus that propagates misinformation. It is admissible under R8 because 374 and 5,858 are both verbatim Table 1 counts with the same denominator and the four categories sum exactly to the total. (2) Denominator choice: 5,858 (the Table 1 analytic sample) rather than the 6,039 answers coded, because the per-category counts are only given for 5,858; the paper does not report how the 181 dropped answers were distributed. (3) CONTENT rather than SHARING: the items are original answers authored on a Q&A platform, i.e. 'all items that exist' from a set of accounts, which the governing rule lists under CONTENT (a platform's posts); the study frames it as content analysis, not as sharing behaviour. (4) denom_selection = curated because the corpus is restricted to the 221 most prolific GMO answerers out of 21,422 users, so it is not a census of GMO answers - it over-represents heavy contributors, and the authors themselves note Zhihu users are 'much more science-savvy compared to the lay public'. Confidence is medium for these two reasons (derived value + heavily curated denominator), not because of any doubt about the counts. QUOTE NOTE: the source_quote is the contiguous Table 1 caption, column headers and N row as the text file renders them; the table note that states '374 answers that propagated misinformation' in prose sits further down the page and cannot be joined to this span contiguously.

missed_or_uncertain: Seen and NOT extracted. (1) 1,809 answers 'discussed about GMO misinformation' (Table 4), i.e. 30.9% of 5,858 - this is the union of propagating, debunking and ambiguous answers, so most of it is NOT misinformation (992 of them debunk it); a share that counts debunking as misinformation would be wrong, and it is also a cross-category sum, which R8 forbids. (2) 992 debunking answers (16.9%) and 443 ambiguous (7.6%) - corrective and neutral content, not misinformation numerators. (3) All Mention Group percentages (full sample 11.7%; misinformation-irrelevant 7.6%; propagate 25.1%; debunk 23.7%; ambiguous 10.6%; pro-GMO/anti-GMO faction mentions 3.9%/8.4% etc.) - these measure identity language, not misinformation. (4) Justification shares in Table 4 (55.3% of Mention Group answers used justification vs 36.5% of those that did not; 40.5% of all misinformation-discussing answers) - a discourse-quality measure computed inside the misinformation-related subset, not a falsity share, so not even a within_misinfo_content row. (5) Risk ratios (propagate 3.45, debunk 3.33, ambiguous 1.49; justification 1.51), all OLS/probit coefficients in Tables 2, 3 and 5, and the dictionary-validation accuracies (anger 0.96, disgust 0.83). (6) The crawl totals 40,101 answers / 21,422 users are frame sizes, not estimates. Note also that Tables 2-5 are badly mangled by the PDF-to-text conversion (columns interleaved with body text); Table 1 and Table 4, which carry the counts used here, are legible and internally consistent, so text_status is 'ok' rather than 'garbled'.

rob.design: Computational content analysis of a Chinese Q&A platform. Zhihu Web Crawler API collected all answers about GM (转基因): 40,101 answers by more than 21,422 unique users as of September 2019, spanning an 8-year time series; purposively restricted to the 221 authors with more than 10 GMO answers, giving 6,039 answers for manual coding (5,858 in the analytic tables after dropping answers with no comment count). Two researchers manually coded Mention Group, Mention Misinformation, attitude toward misinformation (propagate / debunk / ambiguous) and use of justification, against an external reference list of GMO misinformation from Chinese government and science-association sources; intercoder agreement reported as Cohen's kappa 0.812 to 1 across variables. Negativity measured by the Chinese Affective Lexicon Ontology Dictionary (anger, disgust), human-validated at 0.96 and 0.83 accuracy. OLS and probit regressions with follower, following, author badge, text length and year controls. No user-level demographics available; authors acknowledge they cannot know who engages with which content.
